title: Did a Baby Formula Scare in Israel Influence Fertility?
gist: Peter Foreshaw Brookes uses Israel's 2003 kosher baby-formula scare as a natural experiment. Jewish birth rates, but not Muslim ones, fell exactly 12 months later, and the drop was biggest among the groups most dependent on kosher formula. He concludes that 'culture' and 'cost' drivers of fertility interact and cannot be separated, so pronatalist policy has to tackle both.

themes.theme: Formula scare as fertility natural experiment

insights.claim: In November 2003, the Israeli government banned a kosher baby formula that turned out to lack sufficient nutrients and caused the deaths of at least two babies.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/familystudies/
insights.so_what: Product-safety shocks in essential infant goods can have demographic effects well beyond the product itself.
insights.quote: In November 2003, the Israeli government banned a specific kosher baby formula, citing health issues in children using it.

insights.claim: Exactly one year after Israel's 2003 kosher baby-formula scare became public, the country's monthly crude birth rate, which had been rising, began to fall and levelled off about 16% lower.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/familystudies/
insights.so_what: A single scare over the safety of an infant product was followed by a large, lasting drop in births.
insights.quote: Exactly one year after the scare became public, the monthly Israeli crude birth rate, which had been rising, began to fall, plateauing around 16% lower
insights.locator: Exactly one year after the scare

insights.claim: Israel's Muslim birth rate did not change after the 2003 kosher-formula scare, while Jewish birth rates fell 12 months later, which fits roughly 9 months of pregnancy plus 2-4 months to conceive.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/familystudies/
insights.so_what: The timing and the unaffected comparison group make a stronger causal case than simple correlation.
insights.quote: Muslims (who were, we can reasonably assume, not buying kosher formula in the first place) had around the same number of babies after the shock
insights.locator: However, the Muslim birth rate did

insights.claim: After the 2003 kosher-formula scare, fertility in Israeli Jewish subgroups fell in line with their expected use of kosher formula: traditional religious Jews fell most, then orthodox and less-religious traditional Jews, while secular Jews were unaffected.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/familystudies/
insights.so_what: A dose-response pattern like this strengthens the causal reading and argues against confounders such as the intifada.
insights.quote: the higher the expected use of kosher baby formula, the more the growth in the fertility rate for those groups underperformed secular Jews
insights.locator: That is exactly what we see

insights.claim: In 2005, the first full year after Israel's baby-formula scare, the fertility rate fell 5.4% among traditional religious Jews and 2.5% among the ultra-orthodox, while it rose 5.9% among secular Jews.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/familystudies/
insights.so_what: The size of the effect shows how sensitive birth decisions are to the cost and availability of infant care.
insights.quote: By 2005, the first full year after the baby formula scare, traditional religious Jews’ fertility rate fell by 5.4%, and the ultra-orthodox fertility rate fell by just 2.5%

insights.claim: Ultra-orthodox Jews use little baby formula, probably because Orthodox teaching favors breastfeeding, which partly shielded them from the effects of the kosher-formula scare.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/familystudies/
insights.so_what: Cultural practices determine which groups are exposed to supply shocks in consumer goods.
insights.quote: The ultra-orthodox have low rates of formula use (likely on account of Orthodox Jewish teaching in favor of breastfeeding)
insights.locator: The discerning reader might remain unconvinced

insights.claim: Fertility is shaped by many small factors, including whether a friend or colleague recently had a baby, car seat regulations, prior caregiving experience and access to baby formula.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/familystudies/
insights.so_what: Seemingly minor regulations and supply issues can move birth rates measurably.
insights.locator: Fertility can be shaped by all

insights.claim: The baby-formula case shows that 'cultural' and 'economic' drivers of fertility cannot be cleanly separated: breastfeeding norms decided which groups were exposed to formula cost and availability shocks in both Israel and the US.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/familystudies/
insights.so_what: Models that treat fertility as purely economic or purely cultural will misjudge how it responds to policy.
insights.quote: Was it cost or culture? The answer is: both.

insights.claim: The author argues that pronatalist policymakers must both offset the costs of parenting and help family-friendly cultural norms take root, because neither works alone.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/familystudies/
insights.so_what: Effective pronatalist packages will mix subsidies with cultural measures, which affects how much they cost and how they are designed.
insights.quote: they will have to both offset parental costs and ensure that more family-friendly cultural norms are able to take root
insights.locator: The lesson for pronatalists is straightforward
